positions/cessationist-warfare-critique/: Cessationist and sufficiency critique of deliverance ministry
Reformed critique of spiritual warfare
sufficiency of Scripture approach

Satan and demons are real, but the believer’s defence is the whole armour of God — truth, righteousness, faith and the word — not special techniques; Christians cannot be demon-possessed, and the apostolic sign-gifts of exorcism are not normative today.
Christ has decisively defeated Satan; believers resist by faith, Scripture and prayer.
Indwelt by the Spirit, Christians cannot be possessed or “demonised”.
The apostolic sign gifts, including authoritative exorcisms, have ceased or are rare.
Deliverance techniques, binding spirits and spiritual mapping lack biblical warrant.
Ephesians 6:10-18
James 4:7
1 Peter 5:8-9
2 Corinthians 12:12
Hebrews 2:3-4

Grounded in Reformation caution about exorcism rites (Calvin) and B. B. Warfield’s Counterfeit Miracles (1918); restated by evangelical and Reformed critics of deliverance and SLSW and by John MacArthur’s Strange Fire (2013).
Thomas Ice
Richard Mayhue
Many Reformed Baptist and Presbyterian pastors
It keeps Christ’s finished victory and the sufficiency of Scripture central.
It protects vulnerable people from fear, manipulation and abusive practices.
It notes that the New Testament epistles give no instructions for exorcism.
Pentecostals and continuationists argue it is a form of Western rationalism that leaves believers without help against real oppression.
Missionaries in animistic contexts report that cessationist theology often fails to address converts’ fears.
Critics note that Jesus commissioned all disciples to cast out demons.
Cessationists answer that the gospel addresses fear by assurance in Christ and that pastors can pray for the afflicted without techniques.
Many acknowledge real demonic activity, especially in missionary contexts, while rejecting systematised deliverance.
Shapes Reformed and many Baptist churches’ approach to spiritual warfare.
A major voice in evangelical debates over charismatic practice.
positions/ransom-theory/oneLine: Humanity, held captive by the devil through sin, is set free because Christ gave his life as a ransom — in many versions, a "bait" by which the devil overreached himself and lost his rights.
positions/ransom-theory/coreClaims/0: After the fall the devil held humanity in bondage and, in some sense, by right.
positions/ransom-theory/coreClaims/1: Christ’s life was given as the ransom price for captives (Mark 10:45).
positions/ransom-theory/coreClaims/2: The devil, seizing the sinless Christ to whom he had no claim, forfeited his power ("abuse of power"), or was deceived by divinity hidden in flesh (fish-hook).
positions/ransom-theory/coreClaims/3: Salvation is liberation from captivity to sin, death and the devil.
positions/ransom-theory/origin: Hints in Irenaeus (redemption from apostasy); explicit in Origen’s Commentary on Matthew (c.246); developed by Gregory of Nyssa (Catechetical Oration, c.385), Rufinus, Augustine (the cross as "mousetrap") and Gregory the Great; dominant in popular Western imagination until Anselm.
positions/ransom-theory/strongestArgumen: It takes the biblical language of ransom and captivity seriously.
It vividly expresses the cosmic drama of liberation from hostile powers.
It was widely held for a millennium in East and West.
positions/ransom-theory/strongestObjecti: Gregory of Nazianzus: paying a ransom to the robber himself is an outrage.
Anselm and Abelard: the devil has no rights against God; God owes him nothing.
The deception motif seems unworthy of God.
positions/ransom-theory/responses/0: Defenders reply that the "price" language is metaphorical, expressing the costliness of liberation, not a commercial transaction with Satan.
positions/ransom-theory/responses/1: Aulén argued that the ransom imagery is a pictorial form of the deeper "classic" victory idea.
positions/ransom-theory/consequences/0: Shaped early liturgy, art (the harrowing of hell) and drama.
positions/ransom-theory/consequences/1: Absorbed into Christus Victor in the 20th century.
positions/recapitulation/oneLine: Christ, the new Adam, "sums up" and re-lives the whole human story in obedience, undoing at every stage what Adam did, and leads humanity to incorruption and the likeness of God.
positions/recapitulation/coreClaims/0: The incarnate Son passes through every age of human life, sanctifying it.
positions/recapitulation/coreClaims/1: Where Adam disobeyed at a tree, Christ obeyed on the tree; where Eve disobeyed, Mary obeyed.
positions/recapitulation/coreClaims/2: Christ conquers the enemy in the same human nature that was conquered.
positions/recapitulation/coreClaims/3: Salvation is the restoration and completion of the image and likeness of God.
positions/recapitulation/origin: Irenaeus of Lyon, Against Heresies (c.180), especially III.18-23 and V.14-21, against the Gnostic disparagement of creation.
positions/recapitulation/strongestArgume: It integrates incarnation, life, death and resurrection rather than isolating the cross.
It affirms the goodness of creation and the body against Gnosticism.
Its Adam-Christ structure is thoroughly Pauline.
positions/recapitulation/strongestObject: It may leave unclear why the death of Christ in particular is necessary.
Western critics see in it too little attention to guilt and justice.
Some details (e.g. Christ living to old age) are speculative.
positions/recapitulation/responses/0: Irenaeans answer that death is precisely the climax of the recapitulation, where the enemy is defeated in his own domain.
positions/recapitulation/responses/1: Recent scholarship (Wingren, Behr) sees Irenaeus as a biblical theologian of the whole economy, not a speculative one.
positions/recapitulation/consequences/0: Foundational for Eastern soteriology and theosis.
positions/recapitulation/consequences/1: Influential on modern participatory and union theologies.
positions/satisfaction-theory/oneLine: By sin humanity robbed God of the honour due to him and owes a satisfaction it cannot pay; Christ, as God-man, freely offers his sinless life, restoring God’s honour and meriting grace for humanity.
positions/satisfaction-theory/coreClaims: Sin is the failure to render God the honour due to him.
God’s justice and the order of creation require either punishment or satisfaction (aut poena aut satisfactio).
Only God can pay, but only humanity ought to pay — hence the God-man.
Christ’s voluntary death earns a reward he does not need, which he gives to humanity.
positions/satisfaction-theory/origin: Anselm of Canterbury, Cur Deus Homo (completed 1098), drawing on feudal notions of honour and the penitential system of satisfaction; refined by Thomas Aquinas (ST III q. 46-49) as superabundant satisfaction motivated by love.
positions/satisfaction-theory/strongestA: It explains why the incarnation and death of Christ were fitting and necessary.
It takes sin seriously as an offence against God, not only harm to humans.
It decisively rejected the idea that the devil had rights.
positions/satisfaction-theory/strongestO: Abelard and modern critics: it pictures God as a feudal lord concerned for his honour.
Orthodox critics: it isolates the death of Christ from the incarnation and resurrection.
Socinus: if satisfaction is made, forgiveness is not free.
positions/satisfaction-theory/responses/: Defenders argue that God’s "honour" is the right order of creation, not personal vanity, and that God himself provides the satisfaction out of mercy.
Aquinas grounds satisfaction in Christ’s love and obedience rather than the quantity of suffering.
positions/satisfaction-theory/consequenc: Became the dominant Western framework; shaped penance, indulgences and Reformation penal theories.
positions/moral-influence/oneLine: The cross saves primarily by revealing God’s love so powerfully that it awakens repentance and responsive love in human hearts, transforming them.
positions/moral-influence/coreClaims/0: God needs no payment to forgive; the obstacle to reconciliation lies in human hearts.
positions/moral-influence/coreClaims/1: Christ’s life and death display God’s love to the uttermost.
positions/moral-influence/coreClaims/2: That love kindles love in us, freeing us from sin and binding us to God.
positions/moral-influence/coreClaims/3: Redemption is this greater love produced in us by Christ’s passion.
positions/moral-influence/origin: Peter Abelard, Commentary on Romans (c.1133-37); renewed in liberal Protestantism by Schleiermacher, Albrecht Ritschl, Horace Bushnell and Hastings Rashdall (The Idea of Atonement in Christian Theology, 1919).
positions/moral-influence/strongestArgum: It locates the source of atonement firmly in God’s love.
It avoids any suggestion of God being placated by violence.
It addresses the transformation of the person, not only legal status.
positions/moral-influence/strongestObjec: Bernard: it reduces Christ to an example and denies objective redemption.
Why must Christ die if only a demonstration of love is needed? A purposeless death demonstrates nothing (Denney).
It underestimates the power of sin and the need for liberation and forgiveness.
positions/moral-influence/responses/0: Some historians argue Abelard himself also affirmed objective elements (Christ’s merit and intercession).
positions/moral-influence/responses/1: Defenders respond that love that suffers with and for sinners is itself the most objective reality.
positions/moral-influence/consequences/0: Condemned in Abelard’s person at Sens (1141); revived in 19th-century liberalism.
positions/moral-influence/consequences/1: Now commonly included as one dimension of the atonement.
positions/penal-substitution/oneLine: Out of love, God the Son bore in our place the penalty that divine justice decreed against sin, so that God is just in forgiving and justifying sinners.
positions/penal-substitution/coreClaims/: Sin is guilt before God’s holy law and incurs his just wrath and the penalty of death.
Christ, as substitute and representative, bore that penalty and curse in our place.
God’s justice is satisfied and his wrath propitiated; the believer’s guilt is removed and Christ’s righteousness imputed.
The source is God’s love: the Father gives the Son and the Son freely gives himself.
positions/penal-substitution/origin: Penal elements appear in the fathers (e.g. Eusebius, Augustine on Christ bearing our punishment); developed by Luther and Calvin (Institutes II.16, 1559), systematised by Turretin, Owen (1647), the Westminster Confession and Charles Hodge (1872-73); restated by Packer (1974), Stott (1986).
positions/penal-substitution/proponentsO: Steve Jeffery, Michael Ovey and Andrew Sach
positions/penal-substitution/strongestAr: It accounts for texts of curse-bearing, propitiation and "made sin for us".
It shows how God is both just and the justifier (Rom 3:26) and grounds assurance of complete forgiveness.
It expresses substitution as the self-giving of the Triune God, not the punishment of an unwilling third party.
positions/penal-substitution/strongestOb: Socinus and liberals: punishment cannot be transferred; forgiveness that requires payment is not forgiveness.
Christus Victor and Orthodox critics: it makes the Father’s wrath the problem and narrows atonement to a legal transaction.
Feminist and nonviolent critics: it risks portraying "divine child abuse" and sanctifying violence.
positions/penal-substitution/responses/0: Defenders answer that the Father and Son act in one will of love (Stott’s "self-substitution of God").
positions/penal-substitution/responses/1: They argue that penal substitution includes victory and example rather than excluding them, and that wrath is God’s settled opposition to evil, not caprice.
positions/penal-substitution/consequence: Central to Protestant confessional and evangelical preaching, hymnody and assurance.
A major identity marker in modern evangelical debates.
positions/governmental-theory/oneLine: God, as moral governor of the universe, forgives sinners, but displays in Christ’s death what sin deserves, upholding the authority of his law and deterring sin.
positions/governmental-theory/coreClaims: God acts as ruler (rector), not as private creditor or offended party.
The penalty of the law can be relaxed, but not without upholding the law’s honour.
Christ’s suffering is a penal example demonstrating God’s hatred of sin, not an exact equivalent of our punishment.
Forgiveness is then offered conditionally on repentance and faith.
positions/governmental-theory/origin: Hugo Grotius, Defensio fidei catholicae de satisfactione Christi (1617), against Socinus; developed by New England theologians (Joseph Bellamy, Jonathan Edwards Jr.), Charles Finney and Methodist theologians such as John Miley (1879).
positions/governmental-theory/strongestA: It answers Socinus by showing why forgiveness requires the cross without strict transfer of punishment.
It fits an Arminian theology of universal atonement and conditional pardon.
It emphasises God’s moral order and public justice.
positions/governmental-theory/strongestO: Reformed critics: it makes the cross a symbol rather than a real bearing of penalty.
If Christ was not actually punished for our sins, the demonstration seems theatrical.
It may present God more as administrator than as loving Father.
positions/governmental-theory/responses/: Grotians reply that the display is real suffering endured for sin, not mere theatre.
They argue it best preserves both justice and free grace.
positions/governmental-theory/consequenc: Influential in New England theology, Finney’s revivalism and some Wesleyan systematic theology.
